title: One solar eruption squeezed another into a stronger storm
freshness: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal Letters; arXiv version submitted November 13, 2026; preferred 15-day search window.
excerpt: A later solar eruption appears to have squeezed an earlier one as both raced toward Earth in May 2024. Simulations show that the compression preserved a southward magnetic field about twice as strong as it would have been in the first eruption alone.
whyItMatters: Space-weather forecasts need to predict more than whether a solar eruption will reach Earth. This study shows how eruptions can reshape one another in transit, strengthening the magnetic orientation that transfers energy into Earth's magnetic environment.

exploreFurther.label: Wang et al., accepted by The Astrophysical Journal Letters

whatToExploreNext: Why does a southward interplanetary magnetic field connect so efficiently with Earth's magnetosphere?

sources.label: Squeezing Drives Southward Magnetic Field Enhancement During 10 May 2024 CME-CME Interaction

body:
## A storm strengthened on the way

One coronal mass ejection appears to have squeezed another as both raced from the Sun toward Earth, helping create the severe geomagnetic storm of May 10, 2024. A coronal mass ejection, or CME, is a vast cloud of magnetized plasma thrown into space. The new analysis suggests that an eruption's danger can change substantially after it leaves the Sun.

The event began with three similar CMEs from active region 13664 on May 8. The later clouds traveled faster and caught the first one. By the time the combined disturbance reached Earth, it helped produce the strongest geomagnetic storm since 2003, with the global Kp index reaching its maximum value of 9.

Why did the merged structure carry such an effective magnetic punch? The key quantity is Bz, the north-south component of the magnetic field moving with the solar wind. When Bz points south, it can connect with Earth's oppositely directed field at the dayside magnetosphere. That magnetic connection transfers energy into near-Earth space and can drive auroras, satellite drag, navigation errors, and electrical disturbances.

## Replaying three eruptions

The researchers combined images from SUTRI, NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory, SOHO, and STEREO-A with measurements near Earth from the Wind spacecraft. They then used a three-dimensional solar-wind model to follow the eruptions from close to the Sun to Earth's orbit.

The model tested three controlled cases. Two contained interacting CMEs with different magnetic arrangements. The third contained only the first CME, providing a comparison for how it would expand without a later eruption pressing from behind.

In both interaction cases, the second CME first applied extra dynamic pressure, the force of fast-moving plasma. Magnetic and thermal pressure then continued compressing the first cloud. Instead of expanding freely and weakening as it crossed interplanetary space, the first CME became flatter and retained more of its magnetic strength.

Near Earth, the interacting cases produced a southward Bz stronger than 60 nanoteslas. The single-CME control reached only about 30 nanoteslas. In other words, the modeled interaction roughly doubled the field component most effective at driving a geomagnetic storm. The same squeezing appeared even when the researchers reversed the second CME's magnetic handedness, suggesting that compression, rather than one special magnetic alignment, was the main cause.

## Observation and interpretation

The spacecraft data measured the real eruptions, their evolution across telescope fields of view, and the complex magnetic disturbance at Earth. The claim that squeezing preserved the strong southward field comes from the simulation constrained by those observations. It is a physical reconstruction, not a continuous measurement of the clouds all the way from the Sun.

There are useful limits on the result. The event-matching run arrived at Earth about 11 hours too early. The researchers examined one storm and changed only the magnetic handedness of the second CME; other separations, speeds, directions, and field structures could behave differently. Identifying which part of the tangled near-Earth signal belonged to each eruption also depends partly on the model.

Even with those caveats, the comparison points to a forecasting lesson. A CME that looks moderate near the Sun may become more geoeffective if another eruption catches it and prevents its magnetic field from fading. Forecasts therefore need to track the interaction between successive solar eruptions, not just each cloud in isolation.
